brief: Yes. SFT changes parameters and can teach new facts, but low training loss does not prove reliable knowledge acquisition.
detail: A model may memorize the wording of demonstrations while failing on paraphrases, novel combinations, or conflicting evidence. Test on questions that isolate newly introduced information and prevent source leakage. For broad domain exposure, continued pretraining may be appropriate; for changing facts, RAG may be preferable. The slogan “SFT only teaches format” is too absolute, as is the claim that a few examples reliably install arbitrary knowledge.

question: How to select datasets effectively?
originalQuestion: How to select datasets effectively?
brief: Select datasets according to the target task and observed failure modes, then test whether each source adds measurable value.
detail: Audit relevance, answer quality, licensing, duplication, contamination, and coverage. Sample and inspect actual records rather than trusting dataset names or leaderboard popularity. Start with a clean baseline mixture and add sources through controlled ablations. Keep selection decisions separate from the final test set, and monitor whether gains on one slice introduce regressions elsewhere.

question: How to choose a distributed training framework?
originalQuestion: How to choose a distributed training framework?
brief: Choose a distributed training approach from the model's memory needs, cluster interconnect, required parallelism, and operational support.
detail: Data parallelism replicates computation across batches; FSDP and ZeRO shard training states; tensor and pipeline parallelism split computation; expert parallelism distributes MoE experts. PyTorch FSDP, DeepSpeed, and Megatron-based stacks serve different combinations of those needs. Check checkpoint portability, restart behavior, kernel support, and integration with the existing codebase, then benchmark a representative run. See [FSDP2](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/intermediate/FSDP_tutorial.html), [ZeRO](https://www.deepspeed.ai/tutorials/zero/), and [Megatron Core](https://docs.nvidia.com/megatron-core/developer-guide/latest/index.html).

question: What are key LLM training tips?
originalQuestion: What are key LLM training tips?
brief: Validate correctness at small scale, monitor optimization and data quality, and make recovery reproducible before spending a large training budget.
detail: Check token shifting, masks, padding, chat templates, loss normalization, and packed-sequence boundaries. Track gradient norms, numerical overflow, throughput, data mixtures, and held-out quality. Verify a checkpoint can resume with optimizer and data state intact. Use appropriate mixed precision, clipping, and activation checkpointing. Change one major factor at a time so improvements and regressions remain attributable.

question: How to choose model size?
originalQuestion: How to choose model size?
brief: Choose model size jointly with available data, training compute, and deployment requirements.
detail: For dense Transformer pretraining, $C\approx6ND$ is a rough FLOP estimate using parameter count $N$ and training tokens $D$; it omits important details such as long-context attention and exact architecture. Compute-optimal training and inference-efficient deployment can favor different choices. A smaller model trained longer may be useful when serving costs dominate. Treat scaling-law results as experimental guidance under their assumptions, not universal token-per-parameter rules. See [Chinchilla](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556).

question: How to select GPU accelerators?
originalQuestion: How to select GPU accelerators?
brief: Select accelerators by usable memory, sustained workload throughput, memory bandwidth, interconnect, supported precision, and total cost.
detail: Fit the intended sequence length and microbatch with headroom, then measure tokens per second using the actual model and kernels. Multi-GPU training depends heavily on communication, so peak FLOPs alone can be misleading. Include software compatibility, availability, reliability, power, and checkpoint storage. A faster GPU can reduce total cost if it shortens the run enough; a cheaper one can win when utilization or communication limits performance.

question: What is LangChain?
originalQuestion: What is LangChain?
brief: LangChain is a framework and integration ecosystem for building applications and agents around language models.
detail: It provides abstractions for models, messages, tools, prompts, retrieval, and structured outputs. Current LangChain agents use LangGraph for execution and persistence. The framework coordinates application logic; it does not make the underlying model more accurate automatically. Use it where its integrations and orchestration simplify the application, and check the documentation matching the installed version. See the [LangChain overview](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/overview).

question: What are its core concepts?
originalQuestion: What are its core concepts?
brief: Core concepts include models, messages, prompts, tools, retrieval, structured outputs, and execution state; workflows can be deterministic or model-directed.
detail: A deterministic workflow specifies the next operation in code. An agent lets the model choose among permitted actions within a controlled loop. LangGraph supplies explicit stateful orchestration, while LangSmith supports tracing and evaluation. Older tutorials also organize concepts around “chains,” “indexes,” and “memory”; retain the concepts without assuming their historical classes remain the preferred APIs. See [LangChain concepts](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/overview).

question: What are components and chains in LangChain?
originalQuestion: What are components and chains in LangChain?
brief: Components perform individual operations; chains compose operations into a defined flow.
detail: For example, a workflow can format a prompt, call a model, and parse its response. Runnable-style interfaces support composition and invocation across compatible components. A chain can be conditional or parallel, but its control flow is still specified by the application rather than necessarily chosen by an agent. Handle retries and side effects explicitly: retrying a model call is different from repeating a tool that changes external state.

question: What are prompt templates and prompt values?
originalQuestion: What are prompt templates and prompt values?
brief: A prompt template fills named variables into a reusable text or message structure; a prompt value is the formatted result passed to a model.
detail: A chat template can preserve system, user, and assistant roles instead of concatenating everything into one string. Validate required variables and keep user content separate from application instructions. Formatting does not enforce instruction priority or prevent prompt injection. Budget tokens after formatting, especially when inserting history and retrieved documents. The tokenizer's model-specific chat template is a separate serialization layer from an application prompt template.

question: What are example selectors, and when are they useful?
originalQuestion: What are example selectors, and when are they useful?
brief: An example selector chooses which few-shot demonstrations to include for a particular request.
detail: Selectors may use semantic similarity, token budget, diversity, or task metadata. Similar examples can improve relevance, but picking only near-duplicates can narrow behavior or leak answers from an evaluation set. Select demonstrations from an approved training pool, reserve room for the actual request and evidence, and evaluate whether the chosen examples improve outputs compared with a fixed small set.

question: What do output parsers validate, and what do they not validate?
originalQuestion: What do output parsers validate, and what do they not validate?
brief: Output parsers convert model responses into application types and report format errors; they do not establish that the content is true.
detail: A parser might validate JSON fields, types, or an enum. Prefer a model/provider's supported structured-output mechanism when suitable, then validate the returned object and domain constraints. Decide whether malformed output should trigger a bounded retry, repair, or user-visible failure. A syntactically valid amount or citation can still be wrong. See [LangChain structured output](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/structured-output).

question: How do indexes and retrievers differ?
originalQuestion: How do indexes and retrievers differ?
brief: An index organizes data for search; a retriever accepts a query and returns relevant documents or records.
detail: A vector store can back a retriever, but retrieval can also use BM25, a database, an API, or several sources together. Preserve stable IDs, source metadata, and authorization filters. Index construction and query-time retrieval are separate lifecycle stages: changing embedding models usually requires re-embedding compatible documents. A retriever's interface does not guarantee useful recall or proper access control; those require implementation and evaluation.

question: How should chat message history be stored and used?
originalQuestion: How should chat message history be stored and used?
brief: Chat message history stores conversation turns, while the context for a model call is the selected portion of that history and other relevant state.
detail: Store role, content, and tool-call relationships under a correctly scoped conversation identifier. Persistence can outlive a process, but storing messages does not mean every message should be sent on every call. Apply token budgeting, retention rules, and authorization. Current LangGraph-backed agents can checkpoint thread state; cross-conversation memory needs a separately designed storage and retrieval policy. See [short-term memory](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/short-term-memory).

question: What are agents and toolkits?
originalQuestion: What are agents and toolkits?
brief: An agent uses a model to select actions from available tools; a toolkit groups related tools and their interfaces.
detail: A tool exposes a schema and executable behavior, while the agent loop interprets model requests, validates arguments, executes permitted calls, and returns results. Enforce permissions in code, not only in the prompt. Add timeouts, bounded iterations, error handling, and approval points for actions that require them. Use deterministic workflows when the action sequence is known; an agent loop adds flexibility and additional failure modes. See [LangChain agents](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/agents).

question: How can Agents access conversation context?
originalQuestion: How can Agents access conversation context?
brief: Agents access conversation context through explicit state or retrieved memory that the application supplies to each model call.
detail: Combine recent messages, relevant past facts, tool results, and application state within a token budget. Scope storage and retrieval to the correct user and conversation; an embedding similarity score is not an authorization decision. Distinguish short-term thread state from long-term information shared across sessions. Store provenance and support updates or deletion, because old preferences and summaries can become stale. See [LangGraph memory](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/add-memory).

question: When should an agent retrieve the full conversation history?
originalQuestion: When should an agent retrieve the full conversation history?
brief: Loading the full conversation is simple and preserves detail, but only works when the useful history fits the model's context and cost budget.
detail: Retrieve messages in order, preserve system instructions and tool-call/result pairs, and reserve space for new evidence and the answer. Long transcripts increase prefill cost and can distract the model. Never concatenate unrelated users' histories. Full-history storage can still be useful for auditing even when model calls use a smaller, selected context.

question: How does a sliding window manage recent conversation context?
originalQuestion: How does a sliding window manage recent conversation context?
brief: A sliding window retains recent conversation turns to bound context use, but can drop important older facts.
detail: Trim by token budget rather than an arbitrary number of messages, and keep complete tool interactions. Preserve essential instructions and durable task state separately; consider a summary or retrieval for older information. Summaries are lossy and should retain links to original messages when precision matters. Evaluate delayed references such as “use the constraint I gave earlier” to detect failures caused by truncation.

question: How would you implement and validate a document Q&A application using LangChain?
originalQuestion: How would you implement and validate a document Q&A application using LangChain?
brief: Build a minimal RAG application with explicit ingestion, retrieval, prompt construction, generation, and evaluation before adding an agent loop.
detail:
In LangChain, connect document loaders and splitters to an embedding/index backend, expose retrieval, then pass selected source text into a model prompt. Keep ingestion separate from query handling and preserve source IDs throughout. The following is conceptual pseudocode, not a version-specific runnable API example:

```text
index = ingest(parse(documents), chunker, embedding_model)
candidates = retrieve(index, question, user_permissions)
evidence = rerank_and_pack(question, candidates, token_budget)
answer = generate(question, evidence, require_source_ids=True)
return validate_citations_and_support(answer, evidence)
```

Test empty retrieval, deleted documents, conflicting sources, unauthorized evidence, and citations that do not support the answer. Framework composition alone does not enforce these properties. See [LangChain's retrieval guide](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/retrieval).

question: Why do LLMs need an external (vector) knowledge base?
originalQuestion: Why do LLMs need an external (vector) knowledge base?
brief: External knowledge sources provide current, private, or precisely attributable information that a model's parameters may not reliably contain.
detail: A vector database is one option, not a requirement. Lexical search, SQL, document stores, graph queries, and APIs can supply better evidence for some tasks. Retrieval can update information without retraining the generator, but introduces ingestion, authorization, ranking, and evidence-quality requirements. An LLM does not need an external knowledge base for every task, such as rewriting a user-provided paragraph.

question: What’s the overall workflow of LLM+VectorDB document chat?
originalQuestion: What’s the overall workflow of LLM+VectorDB document chat?
brief: Document chat typically ingests and indexes documents offline, then retrieves and assembles evidence before generating a cited answer online.
detail: Offline: parse content, preserve structure and source metadata, chunk, embed, and index. Online: interpret the question, apply access filters, retrieve candidates, rerank, expand relevant context, and pack a bounded prompt. Generate an answer with source references, then check citation validity and support. Log retrieval and generation separately so an incorrect answer can be traced to the actual failing stage.

question: What are the core technologies in a RAG system?
originalQuestion: What are the core technologies in a RAG system?
brief: Core RAG technologies include document parsing, chunking, embeddings or lexical indexing, retrieval, reranking, context assembly, generation, and evaluation.
detail: The important interfaces are often more consequential than any individual library: source IDs must survive parsing, embedding queries must match the index, filters must respect permissions, and citations must resolve to evidence. A useful baseline may combine BM25 with dense retrieval and a reranker. Measure each stage before adding query rewriting, graph traversal, or complex agent orchestration.

question: How to build an effective prompt template?
originalQuestion: How to build an effective prompt template?
brief: An effective RAG prompt states the task, separates instructions from evidence, specifies source attribution, and explains what to do when evidence is insufficient or conflicting.
detail: For example, supply the question and numbered excerpts, require support for factual claims, and ask the model to identify unresolved conflicts. Keep source IDs stable and include dates or titles when they affect interpretation. Avoid filling the context with redundant text. Retrieved content is untrusted data: prompt wording helps, but authorization, tool permissions, and output checks must also exist outside the model.

question: What are the limitations of base LLMs that RAG solves?
originalQuestion: What are the limitations of base LLMs that RAG solves?
brief: RAG can reduce gaps in freshness, access to private documents, and source attribution, but does not eliminate hallucination or reasoning errors.
detail: The generator can only use evidence that exists, is accessible, is retrieved, and fits its context. Stale indexes, missing documents, misleading passages, or poor synthesis can still produce wrong answers. Retrieval is most useful when errors stem from unavailable information; it may not fix weak arithmetic, poor instruction following, or bad task definitions. Compare results with and without retrieval on representative questions.

question: What is RAG?
originalQuestion: What is RAG?
brief: Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves external information and conditions a generative model on it when answering a request.
detail: A retriever finds potentially relevant evidence, and a generator uses that evidence with the question. Contemporary applications often retrieve once and place excerpts in a prompt; others retrieve iteratively or use trained retrieval-generation architectures. The original RAG paper combined parametric generation with a non-parametric document index. Retrieval does not necessarily update model weights. See [Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401).

question: How to obtain accurate semantic representations?
originalQuestion: How to obtain accurate semantic representations?
brief: Obtain useful semantic representations by choosing an embedding model trained for the retrieval task and encoding well-formed, appropriately sized content.
detail: Preserve titles, relevant structure, and language information; avoid splitting an answer from its qualifier or embedding OCR noise. Follow the model's query/document prefixes, normalization, and length limits. Evaluate held-out retrieval before considering domain contrastive fine-tuning. An embedding can represent semantic relatedness without capturing answer relevance, exact identifiers, dates, or negation reliably, so lexical and metadata signals may still be necessary.

question: How to align query/document semantic spaces?
originalQuestion: How to align query/document semantic spaces?
brief: Use query and document encoders trained to share a compatible retrieval space, with matching preprocessing and similarity conventions.
detail: Asymmetric retrieval can use distinct encoders or different query/document prompts; compatibility does not require identical text transformations. Match embedding version, dimensions, normalization, and metric. Training on relevant query-positive-negative triples can improve alignment. Never mix document vectors from one embedding model with arbitrary query vectors from another merely because their dimensions match; migrate or rebuild the index coherently.

question: How to match retrieval model output with LLM preferences?
originalQuestion: How to match retrieval model output with LLM preferences?
brief: Select evidence that supports the answer the generator must produce, rather than optimizing semantic similarity alone.
detail: Train or evaluate the retriever with answer-supporting relevance labels, and rerank query-passage pairs for answerability. Preserve necessary definitions, qualifiers, and surrounding context when packing evidence. End-to-end feedback can improve selection, but a generator's preference for a passage is not proof that it is accurate. Keep retrieval relevance, factual correctness, and answer usefulness as distinct evaluation targets.

question: How to improve results via post-retrieval processing?
originalQuestion: How to improve results via post-retrieval processing?
brief: Post-retrieval processing improves evidence through deduplication, reranking, context expansion, and budget-aware selection.
detail: Remove near-identical chunks, rerank against the specific question, and restore neighboring sentences or parent sections when needed. Enforce authorization before passing candidates to a model or external reranker. Diversify evidence for multi-part questions and preserve source IDs through compression. A compressor can omit a crucial exception, so compare answers against the original evidence and measure changes in recall as well as prompt size.

question: How to optimize generator adaptation to inputs?
originalQuestion: How to optimize generator adaptation to inputs?
brief: Adapt the generator to use supplied evidence through clear prompting, relevant demonstrations, or grounded SFT, and evaluate its behavior under imperfect retrieval.
detail: Train or test on sufficient evidence, missing evidence, distractors, contradictions, and unanswerable questions. Require citations where appropriate and teach calibrated abstention rather than guessing. Avoid datasets where the model can ignore retrieval and answer from memorized shortcuts. Generator adaptation cannot repair an absent source reliably; use error analysis to decide whether the bottleneck is evidence availability or evidence use.

question: What are the benefits of using RAG?
originalQuestion: What are the benefits of using RAG?
brief: RAG can improve freshness, domain coverage, source traceability, and updateability without retraining the generator for every document change.
detail: It also enables access-controlled information use and can reduce unsupported answers when retrieval is good. Costs include ingestion, indexing, retrieval latency, context tokens, and additional failure modes. Benefits are workload-dependent: irrelevant retrieval can worsen an answer. Measure grounded task success and total operating cost, not just whether the architecture contains a vector database.

question: Why is PDF parsing necessary?
originalQuestion: Why is PDF parsing necessary?
brief: PDF parsing converts a page-oriented format into usable text and structure for indexing, retrieval, and citation.
detail: A PDF can store positioned glyphs rather than paragraphs, contain scanned images, or mix both. Extraction must recover reading order, headings, tables, and page references. Scanned text requires OCR or an image-capable parser. Without this step, a retriever may index disconnected columns or omit the very facts needed to answer a question. Retain page and region provenance so extracted claims can be checked against the original.

question: What are the common PDF parsing methods and their differences?
originalQuestion: What are the common PDF parsing methods and their differences?
brief: PDF processing methods include native text extraction, OCR, layout-aware parsing, and multimodal model-based extraction.
detail: Native extraction is often fast for digitally generated PDFs but can lose reading order. OCR recognizes text from page images but can confuse characters. Layout models locate headings, tables, and regions; multimodal models can interpret complex pages but may introduce fabricated content or inconsistent structure. Hybrid pipelines select methods by page type. Evaluate against representative documents and retain visual provenance for uncertain results.

question: What problems exist in PDF parsing?
originalQuestion: What problems exist in PDF parsing?
brief: Common PDF parsing problems include broken reading order, missing text, OCR errors, split tables, repeated headers, and lost structural relationships.
detail: Two-column pages can interleave sentences; ligatures and embedded fonts can corrupt characters; scans can erase decimal points. Captions may detach from figures, and tables can lose row/column associations. Use page-level quality checks, compare suspicious regions with images, and exclude repeated boilerplate where appropriate. Parsing errors propagate into embeddings and answers, so fixing them upstream often matters more than switching generators.

question: Why is table recognition important?
originalQuestion: Why is table recognition important?
brief: Table recognition preserves relationships among values, row labels, column headers, units, and footnotes.
detail: A value such as “12.4” is meaningless without its metric, time period, and units. Flattening a table into arbitrary text can associate it with the wrong row or column. Store a structured representation and a readable serialization with source coordinates. For exact aggregates or arithmetic, retrieve the relevant table and use validated computation instead of relying solely on a language model's interpretation.

question: What are the main methods for recognizing and extracting tables?
originalQuestion: What are the main methods for recognizing and extracting tables?
brief: Table extraction usually combines table detection, cell/structure recognition, text recognition or extraction, and conversion to a structured representation.
detail: Rule-based methods use lines, whitespace, and text alignment. Learned methods detect table regions and infer rows, columns, and spans. OCR supplies text for image-based tables, while native text coordinates can serve born-digital documents. Multimodal extraction is another option, but still needs validation. Complex merged cells, repeated headers, and multi-page tables require explicit handling beyond merely detecting a bounding box.

question: How do traditional table-extraction methods work?
originalQuestion: How do traditional table-extraction methods work?
brief: Traditional table extraction uses ruling lines, intersections, whitespace, and alignment heuristics to infer cells and their text.
detail: Line-based methods work well for clearly bordered tables; text-based methods infer columns and rows from aligned words in borderless layouts. They can be fast and inspectable, but depend on document conventions and tuned tolerances. Merged cells, irregular spacing, skew, and tables spanning pages break simple assumptions. Use visual debugging and structural checks rather than trusting an extraction merely because it returned rows.

question: How can pdfplumber extract text and tables?
originalQuestion: How can pdfplumber extract text and tables?
brief: `pdfplumber` extracts native PDF text and tables using character geometry, lines, and configurable table-detection strategies; it is not an OCR engine.
detail: For a born-digital PDF, inspect `extract_words()` and `extract_text()`, crop a known table region if necessary, and use `find_tables()` or `extract_tables()`. Choose line-based, text-based, or explicit boundaries through table settings. Visual debugging with `debug_tablefinder()` helps tune intersection and alignment tolerances. Validate merged cells and repeated headers against the page image. Scanned pages need an OCR stage or another parser. See the [pdfplumber documentation](https://github.com/jsvine/pdfplumber).

question: Why do we need text chunking?
originalQuestion: Why do we need text chunking?
brief: Chunking creates retrievable units that fit embedding and generation budgets while preserving enough context to interpret the evidence.
detail: Whole documents can dilute relevant information or exceed model limits; tiny chunks can lose definitions and exceptions. Choose boundaries from document structure and expected questions. Preserve parent IDs, headings, and offsets so a small matched chunk can be expanded later. Overlap reduces boundary loss but increases storage and duplicates. Tune chunking with retrieval and answer-quality tests rather than applying a universal token count.

question: What chunking strategies can you implement with regex, spaCy, or LangChain?
originalQuestion: What chunking strategies can you implement with regex, spaCy, or LangChain?
brief: Chunking strategies include fixed token windows, sentence or paragraph boundaries, recursive separators, document structure, semantic segmentation, and parent-child retrieval.
detail: Regex can encode known boundaries; spaCy can identify sentence boundaries; LangChain splitters package token-, character-, or structure-based strategies. These are tools, not inherently different semantic objectives. A character limit is not a token limit. Preserve code blocks, tables, and headings when their structure matters, and test whether overlap or parent expansion improves evidence completeness. See [LangChain text splitters](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/integrations/splitters).

question: Why use LLMs to assist recall?
originalQuestion: Why use LLMs to assist recall?
brief: LLMs can improve recall by rewriting ambiguous queries, generating alternative phrasings, or decomposing a complex question into searchable subquestions.
detail: This helps bridge differences between a user's wording and the source corpus. Keep the original query among the candidates and preserve constraints such as entity names, dates, and negation. Rewrites can drift toward an incorrect interpretation, increasing noise and latency. Measure additional relevant evidence retrieved and downstream answer quality, not simply the number of search calls.

question: How does HyDE work, and what are its limitations?
originalQuestion: How does HyDE work, and what are its limitations?
brief: HyDE generates a hypothetical relevant document, embeds it, and uses that vector to retrieve real documents.
detail: The generated text supplies richer document-like semantics than a short query. It is a retrieval aid, not evidence: the final answer should rely on actual retrieved sources. A wrong hypothetical passage can steer retrieval away from the needed evidence, especially for rare terms or entities, and generation adds latency. Compare with direct and hybrid retrieval on the target corpus. See [Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10496).

question: How does FLARE use active retrieval during generation?
originalQuestion: How does FLARE use active retrieval during generation?
brief: FLARE retrieves during generation when an anticipated next sentence contains low-confidence tokens, then regenerates that sentence using retrieved evidence.
detail: The method predicts upcoming content, uses that content to form a retrieval query, and triggers retrieval based on token-confidence signals rather than only at the start. Query construction must avoid overcommitting to uncertain invented details. Reliable token probabilities may be unavailable through some APIs, and high confidence does not prove factual correctness. It adds retrieval and generation work, so evaluate the quality-latency tradeoff. See [Active Retrieval Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.06983).

question: Why construct hard negative samples?
originalQuestion: Why construct hard negative samples?
brief: Hard negatives train a retriever to distinguish genuinely answer-supporting passages from plausible but irrelevant ones.
detail: For a question about a product's refund deadline, a passage about delivery deadlines may be a useful hard negative. Mine candidates from a current retriever or reranker, then verify that they are actually negative. Unlabeled relevant documents are common false negatives. Mix difficulty levels and monitor held-out recall so training does not specialize only to one miner's mistakes.

question: How do random negatives compare with top-k hard negatives?
originalQuestion: How do random negatives compare with top-k hard negatives?
brief: Random negatives are cheap and diverse but often easy; top-k mined negatives are more confusable but contain more false negatives and selection bias.
detail: Retrieve high-scoring candidates for each training query, remove known positives, and filter or annotate the remaining candidates before treating them as negative. Start with a mixture and refresh mining as the retriever changes. The highest-scoring candidate is not automatically a valid negative. Compare gains on independent queries and track whether the mining procedure overrepresents particular document types.

question: Why evaluate RAG?
originalQuestion: Why evaluate RAG?
brief: Evaluate RAG to determine whether failures come from missing sources, retrieval, context assembly, generation, or the overall application.
detail: A good answer metric alone cannot explain why a system failed. Measure evidence coverage and rank before generation, then answer correctness, support, citation quality, and abstention. Include latency, cost, permission enforcement, and freshness. Use realistic questions and source snapshots so results are reproducible and changes to ingestion or indexing can be regression-tested.

question: What are the evaluation methods, metrics, and frameworks?
originalQuestion: What are the evaluation methods, metrics, and frameworks?
brief: Evaluate retrieval and generation separately, then measure end-to-end task success with references, human judgments, and carefully calibrated automated judges.
detail:
Retrieval metrics include recall@k, precision@k, MRR, and nDCG when relevance labels support them. Generation metrics include answer correctness, faithfulness to evidence, citation precision/coverage, and appropriate abstention. A faithful answer can still be factually wrong if its source is wrong.

Ragas provides evaluation metrics, and LangSmith supports dataset-based evaluation and tracing. LLM judges need rubrics, versioning, and calibration against humans; reference-free scores are not ground truth. Include multi-hop, unanswerable, outdated, and adversarial-source cases. See [Ragas metrics](https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/) and [LangSmith evaluation](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/evaluation).

question: What are the optimization strategies for retrieval and generation modules?
originalQuestion: What are the optimization strategies for retrieval and generation modules?
brief: Optimize the stage responsible for the measured error: source coverage and retrieval, evidence packing, or grounded generation.
detail: For retrieval, improve parsing, chunk boundaries, hybrid search, filters, embeddings, and candidate recall before reranking. For generation, preserve sufficient context, reduce distractors, use clear evidence instructions, and test grounded tuning when needed. Cache only with suitable freshness and access scoping. Change one stage at a time and track quality, latency, and cost on the same evaluation set; adding components everywhere obscures causality.

question: How to enhance context using knowledge graphs (KGs)?
originalQuestion: How to enhance context using knowledge graphs (KGs)?
brief: Knowledge graphs augment context with explicit entities and relationships that can connect evidence across documents.
detail: Resolve the question's entities, traverse relevant typed relationships, and retrieve the source passages supporting those edges. A product-dependency question can follow service-to-library-to-vulnerability links more directly than a single vector lookup. Retain dates, confidence, and provenance for every relationship. An extracted graph can contain errors or omissions, so treat its paths as evidence candidates and verify claims against sources.

question: What are the problems with vector-based context augmentation?
originalQuestion: What are the problems with vector-based context augmentation?
brief: Vector retrieval can miss exact identifiers, relational constraints, multi-hop connections, and facts distributed across chunks.
detail: Semantic similarity does not guarantee answer support. A document about the right topic can concern the wrong date, entity, or exception. Dense indexes also require coordinated updates when embeddings or sources change. Combine lexical search, metadata filters, structured queries, graph traversal, or parent expansion where evaluation shows a gap. These complementary methods have their own costs and should not be added without a demonstrated need.

question: How can KG-based methods improve it?
originalQuestion: How can KG-based methods improve it?
brief: Graph-based retrieval can follow explicit relationships and constraints to find evidence that a standalone similarity search misses.
detail: For example, first identify which team owns a service, then retrieve that team's current escalation policy. This depends on accurate entity resolution, edge typing, and temporal validity. Combine graph candidates with text retrieval and reranking, and pass supporting passages to the generator. Graph construction can lose information or introduce unsupported links, so it is not a universal replacement for vector or lexical search.

question: What are the main pain points in RAG and their solutions?
originalQuestion: What are the main pain points in RAG and their solutions?
brief: The main RAG failure points are missing or corrupted sources, poor candidate retrieval, bad ranking or context assembly, and unsupported generation.
detail: Diagnose them in order: confirm the answer exists in the authorized corpus, inspect parsed text, inspect retrieved candidates, inspect packed context, and finally inspect the generated claims. A missing source needs ingestion work; a lost qualifier needs context repair; a model that ignores available evidence needs generation changes. Maintain examples for each failure class so a fix can be tested at the responsible stage.

question: How do you diagnose missing content in a RAG system?
originalQuestion: How do you diagnose missing content in a RAG system?
brief: If required content is absent from the corpus or was lost during ingestion, retrieval tuning alone cannot recover it.
detail: Check source availability, ingestion logs, parser output, OCR, chunk exclusions, permissions, and index freshness. Compare a known source passage with its indexed representation. Repair or reingest the missing content, then run a targeted retrieval check. If no authorized evidence exists, ask for the source or return an explicit insufficient-evidence response rather than synthesizing a plausible answer.

question: What should you check when relevant documents fail to reach the final context?
originalQuestion: What should you check when relevant documents fail to reach the final context?
brief: When relevant documents do not reach the final context, inspect candidate recall, filters, rank cutoffs, reranking, and context packing separately.
detail: If the document never appears among candidates, improve query interpretation or retrieval coverage. If it appears but is ranked poorly, assess reranking signals and relevance labels. If it ranks highly but disappears from the prompt, inspect deduplication and token-budget logic. Increasing k can improve coverage but also add noise and cost, so measure both retrieval and final answer changes.

question: How do you prevent context loss during retrieval and compression?
originalQuestion: How do you prevent context loss during retrieval and compression?
brief: Context loss happens when retrieval or compression separates a claim from information needed to interpret it, such as a heading, qualifier, or table header.
detail: Retrieve smaller units for matching, then expand to neighboring sentences or a parent section with stable source metadata. Preserve relationships among table cells and retain exceptions during summarization. Inspect the exact packed prompt rather than only the original document. More context is helpful only when it restores missing meaning without overwhelming the generator with irrelevant passages.

question: What should you do when the generator fails to extract an answer from available evidence?
originalQuestion: What should you do when the generator fails to extract an answer from available evidence?
brief: If the answer is present in the supplied evidence but the model fails to extract it, test evidence presentation, question clarity, and generator capability.
detail: Remove distractors, restore structure, identify the relevant section, or request constrained extraction with source spans. Use deterministic parsing or code for exact fields and arithmetic when appropriate. Compare a stronger model or grounded SFT only after confirming retrieval is sufficient. Validate the result against the source; a fluent answer with a citation can still misread a negation or numerical unit.

question: How does RAG-Fusion work, and what are its benefits and tradeoffs?
originalQuestion: How does RAG-Fusion work, and what are its benefits and tradeoffs?
brief: RAG-Fusion generates multiple search queries, retrieves a ranked list for each, and fuses the lists before generation, often with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF).
detail:
For document $d$:

$$
\operatorname{RRF}(d)=\sum_{r:d\in r}\frac{1}{c+\operatorname{rank}_r(d)},
$$

where ranks start at 1 and $c>0$ controls rank sensitivity. Keep stable document IDs, merge repeated results, and usually retain the original query. A document ranking 1st and 3rd in two lists with $c=60$ scores $1/61+1/63\approx0.03227$. RRF combines ranks without needing comparable raw scores; the score is not a relevance probability.

Multiple formulations can improve coverage, but add cost and query-drift risk. RRF alone is a general fusion method and does not require an LLM. See [RAG-Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03367).

question: Why do we need Graph RAG?
originalQuestion: Why do we need Graph RAG?
brief: Graph RAG is useful when answering requires connected entities, multi-hop evidence, or corpus-level themes that independent chunk retrieval may miss.
detail: A dependency-impact question naturally involves paths, while a broad question such as “What recurring problems appear across these reports?” may benefit from community summaries. Simple fact lookup may work better with cheaper lexical or vector retrieval. Graph extraction, resolution, and maintenance add cost, so compare against a strong baseline on questions that actually require relationships or global synthesis.

question: What is Graph RAG and how does it work? Show a code example and use case.
originalQuestion: What is Graph RAG and how does it work? Show a code example and use case.
brief: Graph RAG retrieves graph-connected evidence for generation; Microsoft's GraphRAG additionally builds entity relationships and community summaries for local and global search.

question: How to improve ranking optimization in Graph RAG?
originalQuestion: How to improve ranking optimization in Graph RAG?
brief: Improve Graph RAG ranking by combining entity relevance, relationship relevance, path quality, source support, and ordinary text-retrieval signals.
detail: Restrict traversal to useful relation types and hop counts, reduce domination by generic high-degree nodes, and account for dates and extraction confidence. Rerank candidate paths and their supporting passages against the question, then diversify within a token budget. Evaluate answer-supporting evidence rather than only graph connectivity. A short path or popular entity is not automatically the most relevant source.

question: What is fine-tuning, and how is it performed?
originalQuestion: What is fine-tuning, and how is it performed?
brief: Fine-tuning continues training from a pretrained checkpoint on a new objective or dataset to adapt its behavior or capabilities.
detail: Prepare and split the data, preserve tokenizer and input conventions, choose trainable parameters, and optimize with conservative settings. Full fine-tuning updates all selected model weights; parameter-efficient methods train a smaller subset or added modules. Evaluate task gains and retained capabilities, and export the exact tokenizer, configuration, and weight or adapter artifacts required for inference.

question: Why do we need PEFT?
originalQuestion: Why do we need PEFT?
brief: PEFT reduces the trainable parameter and optimizer-state footprint of adapting a large model, making task-specific tuning and checkpoint storage more manageable.
detail: Keeping the backbone frozen avoids gradients and optimizer moments for those weights, though forward computation and many activations still consume resources. Small adapters also let several tasks share a base checkpoint. PEFT does not make the base model disappear from memory or guarantee full-tuning quality. QLoRA further reduces backbone storage through quantization; it is a particular method, not a property of every PEFT technique. See [QLoRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314).

question: What is PEFT and its advantages?
originalQuestion: What is PEFT and its advantages?
brief: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning trains a limited subset of parameters or small added modules while freezing most pretrained weights.
detail: Examples include bottleneck adapters, LoRA, and learned prompts or prefixes. LoRA represents a matrix update as $\Delta W=BA$ with rank $r$, using $r(d_{\mathrm{in}}+d_{\mathrm{out}})$ parameters rather than $d_{\mathrm{in}}d_{\mathrm{out}}$. Benefits include smaller task artifacts and lower optimizer memory. Quality, activation memory, and inference overhead depend on the method; LoRA updates can often be merged into a compatible dense weight matrix. See [LoRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685).

question: Why use adapter-tuning?
originalQuestion: Why use adapter-tuning?
brief: Bottleneck adapter tuning adds small trainable modules to a frozen backbone, allowing multiple tasks to reuse the same pretrained model.
detail: Each task stores its own adapter parameters instead of a full copy of all model weights. This can reduce training-state memory and simplify task switching, especially when data is limited. Extra modules still require computation and can add latency. Choose adapter placement and width using held-out task quality and serving constraints. See [Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning for NLP](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.00751).

question: What’s the core idea behind adapter-tuning?
originalQuestion: What’s the core idea behind adapter-tuning?
brief: A classic adapter projects hidden states down to a small bottleneck, applies a nonlinearity, projects back up, and adds a residual connection.
detail:
A schematic form is:

$$
h'=h+W_{\mathrm{up}}\phi(W_{\mathrm{down}}h+b_{\mathrm{down}})+b_{\mathrm{up}},
$$

where the bottleneck width $r$ is much smaller than model width $d$. The projection weights contribute about $2dr$ parameters. Placement and normalization vary by method. This nonlinear bottleneck module differs from LoRA's low-rank linear weight update, even though both are often loosely called “adapters.” See the [adapter paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.00751).

question: How does classic adapter tuning differ from full fine-tuning?
originalQuestion: How does it differ from full fine-tuning?
brief: Full fine-tuning updates the backbone's weights, while classic adapter tuning freezes the backbone and trains added task-specific modules.
detail: Full tuning offers broader parameter freedom but usually needs more gradient and optimizer memory and a full task checkpoint. Adapter tuning stores a smaller task artifact but still loads the base model and may add inference computation. Neither guarantees better generalization. Classic nonlinear adapters generally cannot be merged into an existing linear weight the way a standard LoRA update can; deployment behavior depends on the method.
